questions.stemMarkdown:
A housing association uses AI to prepare account-correction letters from approved rent records. The letters may change a resident's balance or promise a repayment arrangement. AI creates drafts only. Before release, an authorized reviewer must check each proposed adjustment and promise against the underlying records and approve the letter.

The service manager currently reviews 40 letters a day. Each full check takes three minutes, and she has two hours available. Next month, the expected volume rises to 80 letters a day. A deputy has the same approval authority and could provide another two hours if the director reallocates her duties. Administrative clerks can check arithmetic, but cannot approve adjustments or repayment promises.

The drafting process has performed well, and clerks already catch most numerical errors. The director wants the higher volume handled within the working day. She wants to preserve the existing release standard while making the workflow practical, rather than leaving a review requirement that staff cannot actually complete.

Which redesign best meets those requirements?

options.textMarkdown: Have clerks check every source record and let the manager approve a consolidated summary. This uses existing staff while keeping final approval with an authorized person.
Allocate the deputy to share the full checks, record both reviewers in the workflow, and confirm that their available time covers the expected daily volume.
Have AI perform a second check, with the manager reviewing exceptions and the deputy reviewing a sample of other letters before the daily batch is released.
Have the manager approve standard letter templates, then let clerks release letters that match them. Reserve the deputy for unusual adjustments and repayment arrangements.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Eighty full checks require 240 minutes. The manager and deputy together provide exactly 240 minutes of authorized review, preserving the required check of every adjustment and promise before release.

optionExplanations.A: A consolidated summary does not provide the required authorized check of each adjustment and promise.
optionExplanations.B: The deputy has the needed authority and adds the two hours required to cover all 80 full checks.
optionExplanations.C: A second AI check and sampling replace the required full authorized review of every letter.
optionExplanations.D: Approved templates do not authorize clerks to approve each actual adjustment or repayment promise.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A repair-service team asked AI to identify every request needing a callback under a written checklist. A callback is needed when the customer reports that a repair failed or asks for a promised update. The supervisor then checked the original text of every request AI selected. She has not reviewed any unselected requests, and no other process has checked them.

| Recorded result | Number of requests |
| --- | ---: |
| Requests supplied to AI | 360 |
| Requests selected for a callback | 36 |
| Selected requests checked against the original text | 36 |
| Checked selections that met the checklist | 36 |
| Unselected requests checked against the checklist | 0 |

The AI-generated review note states:

> All selected requests were confirmed. The system therefore identified every request needing a callback, and the remaining 324 requests can be closed without further callback review.

Which assessment is best supported by the recorded evidence?

options.textMarkdown: The review establishes a 10% callback rate for this intake. Further checking would assess consistency, rather than change the conclusion that 36 requests required follow-up.
The review supports the selection method because all chosen cases qualified. Checking another intake would be the strongest way to confirm that this intake was fully covered.
The selections are supported, but closure should wait until a second model independently returns the same callback list. Agreement would substantiate coverage of this intake.
The 36 selections are supported, but coverage remains unknown. Review unselected requests against the checklist before treating the note as evidence that none were missed.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Checking all 36 selected cases supports their correctness. With none of the 324 excluded cases reviewed, it does not establish that every qualifying callback was found.

optionExplanations.A: Ten percent is the observed selection rate, not a verified callback rate for the entire intake.
optionExplanations.B: Another intake cannot establish whether qualifying requests were missed in this intake.
optionExplanations.C: Agreement between models does not check excluded requests against the actual checklist.
optionExplanations.D: Reviewing unselected requests addresses the unanswered coverage question directly.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A community sports trust is reconciling membership renewals. Its policy permits member-level records for this purpose only in its managed AI workspace. Other routes require separate approval. Member IDs are needed to match renewals to existing accounts; the analysis does not decide eligibility or contact members.

The table records actions in execution order. No member records entered any AI system before step 4. The permissions described in step 3 were actually applied before processing began.

| Step | Checkpoint | What was recorded or done |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Task and ownership | AI would prepare a draft reconciliation. The membership officer would verify matches and unresolved cases against the source records before updating accounts. |
| 2 | Data classification | The privacy officer classified the member IDs and renewal rows as internal personal data, and confirmed that the authorized renewal purpose covered this reconciliation. |
| 3 | Capability and access | Security inspected the provider’s built-in file-processing capability and approved it for this task. Access was limited to the supplied renewal files, with account updates, messages, and unrelated files unavailable. |
| 4 | Processing route | Because the managed workspace's upload queue was slow, the analyst uploaded the records through a personal temporary chat in the same AI product, without separate route approval. |
| 5 | Accuracy check | The analyst accepted the computed renewal total after comparing it with a second total generated by the same AI; neither total was tested against independently known results. |
| 6 | Final use | The membership officer began the planned source checks. No account updates or member messages had yet occurred. |

At which step does the process FIRST depart from the stated policy or course-supported method?

options.textMarkdown: Step 2: retaining member IDs prevents the rows from becoming anonymous. The privacy officer should have required aggregate data before allowing a renewal analysis.
Step 5: agreement between two AI-generated totals does not provide an independent known-answer check. The analyst has not yet substantiated the computed renewal figure.
Step 4: the temporary conversation is a different processing route. Its privacy controls do not supply the separate authorization required for these member-level records.
Step 3: limiting access to supplied files prevents meaningful reconciliation. Security should have granted account-update access so the capability could complete the entire workflow.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Step 4 is the first departure: member records entered an unapproved route. Step 5 also lacks a known-answer check, but occurs later; valid purpose, necessary identifiers and actual access restrictions were already established.

optionExplanations.A: Identifiers are necessary for matching; the stated policy permits them in the approved managed route.
optionExplanations.B: This identifies a later verification failure, rather than the first departure.
optionExplanations.C: A personal temporary chat lacks the separately required route authorization despite belonging to the same product.
optionExplanations.D: Read-only reconciliation can prepare matches for the officer; account-update authority is unnecessary for the AI task.

questions.stemMarkdown:
An archive coordinator wants duplicate downloads moved into a review folder. Under the archive rule, files are duplicates only when their complete contents are identical. The most recently filed copy must remain in place. Files with different contents must remain separate, even when their names or sizes match. If filing order cannot be established, that group must stay untouched and be listed for the coordinator.

The approved folder is backed up. The coordinator will inspect a complete move manifest before authorizing any changes. The proposed prompt is:

> Work only in the approved archive folder. Group duplicate files by matching filename and file size. Keep the newest filed copy and propose moving the others into the review folder. If filing dates are missing or tied, use the order of files in the folder listing. Show every proposed move and wait for approval. Leave other files unchanged.

Which TWO independent revisions make the prompt comply with the duplicate and uncertainty rules while preserving the requested workflow?

options.textMarkdown: Base duplicate groups on verified equality of complete file contents, rather than filename and size. Keep the existing manifest and approval step before any movement.
Compare extracted text and document titles to identify equivalent copies, including differently named files. Retain the newest filing date and show the resulting groups for approval.
Use the earliest dated copy when filing dates are tied or missing, recording that fallback in the manifest so the coordinator can inspect it before approval.
Leave a duplicate group untouched when its filing order is unresolved. List the uncertainty separately instead of choosing a retained copy from the folder listing.
Ask a second model to review the proposed duplicate groups and date choices against the manifest. Move only groups where both models agree after coordinator approval.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The duplicate rule requires equality of complete contents, and unresolved filing order requires leaving the group untouched. A and D correct those two independent defects while retaining the full manifest and approval gate.

optionExplanations.A: Verified complete-content equality applies the actual duplicate definition and preserves approval before movement.
optionExplanations.B: Equivalent extracted text or titles does not prove complete file contents are identical.
optionExplanations.C: Choosing an earliest copy is an unauthorized fallback when filing order is unresolved.
optionExplanations.D: Leaving unresolved groups untouched and listing them follows the explicit uncertainty rule.
optionExplanations.E: Model agreement cannot substitute for content equality or authorize a fallback contrary to the archive rule.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A museum communications team is choosing one AI configuration for batches of 30 short exhibition briefs. All three configurations are approved for the same source material. In matched trials, staff used the same brief and review standard. After the recorded verification and repairs, every final batch met that standard. The table shows the complete work required; there were no additional steps.

Each batch must be ready within 28 minutes. Only 18 minutes of staff review time are available, and the tool charge must stay within $3 per batch. Generation finishes before review begins, so those times are added when planning turnaround. The team cannot add staff or reduce the review standard.

The next batches are expected to have the same size and task mix. The team wants the lowest tool cost among the tested configurations that satisfy all three limits. It will use these measurements as planning estimates and continue monitoring actual results.

| Configuration | Generation time | Staff verification and repair time | Tool charge per batch |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| K | 2 minutes | 36 minutes | $0.40 |
| L | 6 minutes | 20 minutes | $1.30 |
| M | 10 minutes | 17 minutes | $2.50 |

Which choice is best supported by these trials and operating limits?

options.textMarkdown: Choose K because its low generation cost leaves room for verification. Keep the existing review standard and use the observed repair time when scheduling each batch.
Choose L because its measured total turnaround is shortest and its cost is lower than M. Keep the full verification and repair process used in the trials.
Choose M because its measured generation and review work fit both time limits and the budget. Confirm those conditions continue to hold on later batches.
Generate with K and ask L to repair the drafts before staff review. Use their individual trial times to plan a cheaper combination within the limits.

questions.explanationMarkdown: M takes 27 minutes overall, uses 17 staff minutes and costs $2.50, satisfying every limit. L takes 26 minutes but exceeds the 18-minute staff allowance; K exceeds both time limits. An untested combination has no measured review requirement.

optionExplanations.A: K needs 38 total minutes and 36 staff minutes, exceeding both limits despite its low charge.
optionExplanations.B: L meets turnaround and budget but requires 20 staff minutes, exceeding the available 18.
optionExplanations.C: M is the only tested configuration satisfying all three limits; continued monitoring treats the trial as an estimate.
optionExplanations.D: The trials do not establish the performance or staff repair time of a K-plus-L workflow.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A consultancy prepares reports for two clients using the same AI account. The same analysts are authorized to work on both clients, and both clients' material is approved for the available environment. Their reporting conditions differ: one requires every statement of a service commitment to cite its contract section; the other requires unresolved commitments to be listed separately for discussion.

The report layout and assembly procedure are otherwise identical. Analysts currently start new chats and paste whichever client instructions and reference files they remember. During staff rotation, one report inherited the other client's treatment of unresolved commitments. The procedure itself was followed correctly.

The available setup supports shared Projects with their own instructions and reference files, account-wide custom instructions, and reusable Skills. The director wants each client’s chats to start with only that client’s standing rules, including chats that do not run the report procedure. She wants one maintainable assembly procedure. General preferences, such as concise language, should still apply across unrelated work.

Which configuration best meets those needs?

options.textMarkdown: Use a separate shared Project for each client’s rules and references, keep the common assembly procedure in a reusable Skill, and reserve custom instructions for global preferences.
Keep both clients in one shared Project and require a client-name field in each request. Store both rule sets beside the references and use one assembly Skill.
Put each client’s reporting conditions inside a separate assembly Skill, leaving Projects for reference files. Let each analyst choose the appropriate Skill when starting a new chat.
Put both client rule sets in account-wide custom instructions with a client-name condition. Keep the common procedure reusable and attach each client’s reference files when needed.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Client-specific rules must apply to every chat for that client, so they belong in separate Projects. The common assembly procedure belongs in a Skill, while global style preferences belong in custom instructions.

optionExplanations.A: Separate Projects isolate standing client context, one Skill preserves the reusable method, and global preferences remain account-wide.
optionExplanations.B: A name field in a shared Project does not meet the requirement to begin with only one client's rules.
optionExplanations.C: Skill-only client rules are absent from client chats that do not invoke the reporting procedure.
optionExplanations.D: Account-wide client rules load both clients' conditions globally and depend on request-time selection.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A training coordinator has been producing workshop handouts in one AI conversation. The initial brief required a short safety reminder on every handout and used an attached, current policy. The first twelve handouts followed that requirement. After many rounds of alternative examples, discarded drafts, and unrelated planning notes, recent handouts have omitted the reminder.

The coordinator checks the original brief: the reminder, audience, source policy, and output format were all clearly specified. The source policy is still current, and the model and enabled features have not changed. Restating the reminder once in the existing conversation fixes one handout, but the omission returns later. The same task is still within the model's demonstrated capabilities.

She suspects the accumulated conversation is contributing to the problem, but timing alone does not establish the cause. She wants a small comparison that can test that explanation before changing shared instructions, replacing the model, or redesigning the handout workflow.

Which next step provides the clearest confirmation test?

options.textMarkdown: Ask for a summary of the conversation and continue in the existing session. Compare the next handout with the last one to see whether summarization improves compliance.
Use a more capable model on the full conversation, preserving the existing source and brief. Compare its next handout with the recent drafts before changing configuration.
Promote the reminder to a shared standing instruction, then repeat the handout in the current conversation. Check whether the new configuration prevents another omission.
Run the same task and brief in a fresh conversation with the current policy and only necessary task facts. Compare reminder compliance without changing the model.

questions.explanationMarkdown: A fresh session with the same model, complete brief and current policy isolates accumulated conversation as the suspected contributor. It is a confirmation test, rather than proof of the cause based on timing alone.

optionExplanations.A: Summarizing within the existing session does not cleanly remove the accumulated context being tested.
optionExplanations.B: Changing the model changes a second variable and does not isolate conversation effects.
optionExplanations.C: Changing shared configuration before testing introduces a new variable and may conceal the original cause.
optionExplanations.D: The controlled fresh-session comparison tests context accumulation while preserving the demonstrated task and model.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A studio asks AI to calculate billed courier costs for completed shipments and compare the result with a $200 budget. Canceled shipments must be excluded. All figures are in dollars; quoted charges are estimates, while billed charges are the amounts actually charged.

| Shipment | Status | Quoted charge | Billed charge |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| P1 | Completed | 45 | 40 |
| P2 | Completed | 60 | 55 |
| P3 | Canceled | 25 | 0 |
| P4 | Completed | 45 | 35 |
| P5 | Completed | 50 | 40 |

The visible execution record confirms that code ran, read all five records, and summed the quoted-charge column without filtering status. It produced 225. The assistant reports:

> The code processed all five records without an error. Courier costs were $225, which is $25 over budget. I also checked that the five quoted charges add to $225, confirming the report.

Which TWO conclusions are supported by the request, source records, and execution evidence?

options.textMarkdown: The agreement between the code result and the added quoted charges validates the reported cost. The budget comparison can be accepted while billing differences are noted separately.
The record establishes that code executed and read every shipment. It does not establish that the calculation used the requested charge measure or eligible shipment set.
Removing the canceled shipment’s quoted charge gives $200, bringing the report into line with the requested shipment set and showing that the budget was exactly used.
The unsupported overspend indicates a code-execution failure. A second execution of the same sum would be needed before using the records to revise the reported figure.
The requested billed total is $170, which is $30 below budget. The source records do not support the reported $25 overspend, despite the successful execution.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The log proves execution and input reading, but the code summed the wrong measure and included an ineligible shipment. Completed billed charges total 40 + 55 + 35 + 40 = $170, which is $30 below the $200 budget.

optionExplanations.A: Reproducing the quoted sum verifies the wrong calculation, not the requested billed cost.
optionExplanations.B: Execution and complete reading are established independently of whether the calculation follows the business rules.
optionExplanations.C: Removing the canceled quote gives $200 in quoted charges, still the wrong charge measure.
optionExplanations.D: The code executed successfully; the defect is its calculation procedure, not failure to run.
optionExplanations.E: The eligible billed charges total $170, so the reported overspend is unsupported.

questions.stemMarkdown:
An art-school administrator commissioned a small studio-reservation prototype through AI. It runs in one browser, uses made-up booking data, and helps staff test the form layout and scheduling rules. Staff checked the examples by hand, including a deliberately conflicting reservation, and the prototype handled those examples correctly.

The school now wants students to log in from different devices, see only their own bookings, and pay reservation fees. Double bookings must be prevented when two students request the same studio at once. Confirmed bookings must survive browser closure, and somebody must be responsible for recovering the service when it fails. These are required features, rather than possible future additions.

The prototype currently has no account isolation, shared persistent booking store, payment integration, or recovery process. The administrator can continue refining it with AI, and the approved development environment permits that work. She needs to choose how to carry the project forward while preserving the useful prototype and addressing the changed scope.

Which approach best fits the new requirements?

options.textMarkdown: Extend the prototype with a shared booking file and student logins, then launch a small pilot. Let staff resolve conflicts and verify payments after confirmation.
Use the prototype to settle requirements, then develop and validate the service through an engineering workflow covering accounts, shared state, payments, recovery, and named operational ownership.
Build student accounts and payments around the prototype, store each student’s bookings in their browser, and appoint staff to recover booking records from daily exports.
Ask a stronger coding model to add all required functions in one pass. Approve release when login, booking, and payment examples succeed in the prototype environment.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Accounts, shared durable state, concurrent bookings, payments and recovery make this a service others depend on. The prototype remains useful for requirements, but release needs an engineering workflow and named operational ownership.

optionExplanations.A: Post-confirmation conflict and payment checks do not satisfy prevention and payment requirements before confirmed bookings.
optionExplanations.B: An engineering workflow addresses all required service properties while retaining the prototype's value.
optionExplanations.C: Per-browser booking storage does not provide shared state, durable centralized records or reliable conflict prevention.
optionExplanations.D: A few successful examples do not validate concurrent behavior, isolation, persistence or operational recovery.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A mentor is writing a reference letter for a volunteer applying to a small leadership programme. She made the assessment herself and supplied her own notes through an approved AI route. AI drafted most of the letter, including the narrative connecting the volunteer's examples to the programme's criteria. The mentor then checked every factual claim, removed an unsupported example, and confirmed that the recommendation expresses her own judgment.

The programme values a mentor's personal account of working with the applicant. Its forms ask the mentor to sign the reference, but do not settle whether drafting assistance must be disclosed. The mentor has checked the relevant organizational and programme rules; none requires or prohibits disclosure, and there is no unresolved legal or contractual issue.

She will retain responsibility for the signed recommendation. She wants to communicate accurately about the assistance because the recipient could reasonably understand the letter as personally composed, not merely personally approved.

Which disclosure choice best fits this situation?

options.textMarkdown: Sign the checked letter without a drafting note, because the mentor owns its claims and judgment. Her verification makes the composition method immaterial to the recipient.
State that AI evaluated the volunteer’s suitability and drafted the reference, while the mentor verified the facts and approved its recommendation before signing the letter.
State briefly that AI assisted with drafting and that the mentor checked and owns the assessment. Describe its actual role without presenting the judgment as delegated.
Add the organization’s general statement that staff may use AI tools. Keep the letter’s specific assistance unstated because the published notice already describes the possible process.

questions.explanationMarkdown: No mandatory disclosure rule settles the case, so the recipient's reasonable understanding matters. AI substantially assisted composition; a brief accurate disclosure preserves the mentor's ownership of the assessment without attributing judgment to AI.

optionExplanations.A: Verification establishes ownership of claims, but does not make substantial drafting assistance immaterial to perceived authorship.
optionExplanations.B: AI did not assess suitability; this statement misrepresents its role in the mentor's judgment.
optionExplanations.C: This discloses actual drafting assistance and accurately retains human assessment and responsibility.
optionExplanations.D: A general organizational notice does not explain AI's actual substantial role in this particular reference.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A training coordinator asks AI to report whether 28 staff members who attended a workshop have earned its certificate. The attendance register confirms that all 28 attended. Their assessment scores have not yet been supplied.

The current provider handbook is the authoritative source for the certificate rule. Its complete relevant passage states:

> Workshop attendance satisfies the participation requirement. A certificate is issued to participants who also score at least 70% in the assessment. Participants below 70% may take one further assessment.

The AI report cites this passage and states:

> All 28 staff have completed the workshop and therefore qualify for certificates. The provider allows a further assessment for participants who want to improve their scores.

The coordinator must decide what the report can currently say about certificate eligibility.

Which revision is best supported by the cited passage and available records?

options.textMarkdown: Confirm attendance and list all 28 as provisionally qualified, with certificates pending score entry. Keep the further assessment as an optional improvement opportunity for participants.
Remove the eligibility finding and request assessment scores. Retain the further-assessment statement because the handbook confirms that another assessment is available to workshop participants.
Confirm attendance, leave certificate eligibility unresolved pending scores, and limit the further-assessment statement to participants below 70%, as specified in the cited rule.
Classify the 28 as currently ineligible because their scores are absent. Replace the improvement statement with the handbook’s further-assessment condition and update eligibility when scores arrive.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Attendance proves participation only. Scores are required to determine the 70% condition, and the further assessment is available specifically to participants below 70%, rather than an unrestricted improvement opportunity.

optionExplanations.A: Provisional qualification is unsupported without assessment scores, and the retake statement remains too broad.
optionExplanations.B: Removing the eligibility conclusion is appropriate, but retaining an unrestricted retake statement misstates the condition.
optionExplanations.C: This preserves confirmed attendance, leaves unknown eligibility unresolved and restores the precise retake condition.
optionExplanations.D: Missing scores establish uncertainty, rather than proof that the participants are ineligible.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A food-bank coordinator wants a handover note for volunteers starting the evening shift. It should tell them what to do about overdue packing requests. The approved request log gives each request’s age, recorded next step, and responsible person; some entries have no person assigned. Volunteers cannot create assignments themselves.

The current prompt is:

> Use the request log to write a short, professional evening handover. Explain the overdue work and make the note helpful. Stay within 150 words and use only the supplied records.

The last note described the backlog clearly but used phrases such as “coordinate follow-up” without saying what a volunteer should do. It also grouped assigned and unassigned requests together. The coordinator’s feedback was “too general; make it more practical.”

The word limit and source restriction will remain.

Which TWO compatible additions supply concrete content requirements addressing the observed failures?

options.textMarkdown: Write for volunteers beginning this shift, using direct instructions for the immediate work they can perform. Link each instruction to the relevant overdue request in the log.
Rank the overdue requests by age and show their request IDs in that order. Include the size of the backlog so volunteers can judge its urgency.
Use the approved handover’s calm tone and short sentences as a style example. Check the revision for clarity and remove wording that sounds abstract or formal.
For each overdue request, state its recorded next step and responsible person. Where no person is recorded, mark assignment as unresolved for the coordinator instead of inventing one.
Add a brief explanation of the log’s status terms and distinguish overdue from completed work. Use consistent labels so volunteers can interpret the summary without specialist knowledge.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The failures concern actionable instructions and ownership, rather than tone or urgency alone. A specifies audience-appropriate actions linked to requests; D adds the recorded next step and owner while leaving missing assignments for the coordinator.

optionExplanations.A: Immediate request-linked actions address the vague instruction problem for evening volunteers.
optionExplanations.B: Ranking by age and reporting backlog size do not specify the actions or unresolved assignment handling.
optionExplanations.C: A style example may improve tone but does not supply the missing content requirements.
optionExplanations.D: Recorded next steps and owners make the handover operational without inventing assignments volunteers cannot create.
optionExplanations.E: Explaining labels does not establish what volunteers should do or separate unassigned work.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A design studio is considering a slide-formatting extension built by its own research team. It would apply the studio’s fonts and spacing to a supplied deck. The deck is approved for AI processing, and a designer will review the result before release. The extension has not been enabled in the design team’s environment.

Security has verified the publisher and opened the package. The formatting code matches the stated task, but the package also includes a search utility used by the research team. In the proposed session, that utility could read every mounted project folder. It has no sending or deletion capability. The format task needs only the supplied deck and the approved style file.

The publisher offers to disable the search utility, and security can restrict the session’s mounted files. A demonstration on invented slides produced the correct layout. The studio wants to decide whether the extension is ready to use on its real project.

Which assessment best fits the evidence and the proposed task?

options.textMarkdown: Proceed after disabling the search utility and verifying that the session can reach only the deck and style file. Keep the planned designer review of formatting.
Proceed after disabling the search utility and adding a formatting-only instruction. The verified publisher and inspected code make the existing mounted folders acceptable for this task.
Proceed in the existing session with the search utility retained but unused. Confirm through a monitored trial that the extension opens only the required deck and style file.
Proceed after obtaining the research team’s documented approval of the package. Retain its tested environment and add a designer check of the resulting slide layout.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Trusted publication and correct formatting do not establish proportionate reach. Disable the unrelated utility and verify session access is limited to the deck and style file before processing real work; retain output review.

optionExplanations.A: Removing the utility and restricting actual reach supplies the missing capability controls.
optionExplanations.B: An instruction to format only does not technically remove access to unrelated mounted folders.
optionExplanations.C: An unused but enabled utility retains unnecessary capability; one observed run does not narrow that reach.
optionExplanations.D: Research-team approval does not establish fit for this team's files and task.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A distributor uses one shared AI workspace to draft product sheets. Its product manager issues a dated catalogue every month. The catalogue is the sole authority for current dimensions and stock codes. The drafting procedure and writing rules change rarely.

Last month’s catalogue and this month’s replacement are both visible in the workspace. Some drafts combine their dimensions. The product manager wants one active authority for drafting, a separately accessible archive, and a visible record of which catalogue supplied each draft. Staff must not maintain a second copy of the product values inside another configuration file.

The four proposals below can all be implemented in the available workspace.

| Proposal | Active drafting material | Update and trace method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R | Latest catalogue in the reference store; stable rules and procedure separately | Replace the active catalogue, archive the superseded version outside drafting retrieval, and record the catalogue version on each draft |
| S | All catalogue versions in the reference store; newest-date preference in the rules | Add each new catalogue and record whichever version the draft cites |
| T | Product values copied into the procedure; catalogues held in the archive | Update the procedure’s values each month and record its release date |
| U | Latest catalogue in the reference store; selected dimensions copied into standing rules | Replace the catalogue monthly, update copied dimensions, and record both dates |

Which proposal meets the maintenance and traceability requirements?

options.textMarkdown: Choose S because its date preference selects current information while preserving comparison material. Recording the cited version gives the product manager an inspectable source trail.
Choose T because a versioned procedure keeps the drafting steps and product values together. Monthly releases provide a clear update event and reduce retrieval ambiguity.
Choose U because current dimensions in standing rules reinforce the catalogue. Recording both dates makes discrepancies visible and lets staff check whether updates were coordinated.
Choose R because it keeps one active product reference, retains history separately, and records the source version without duplicating changing product values in behavioural configuration.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Current product values are reference material, while stable behavior and procedure remain separate. R supplies one active catalogue, archives old material outside retrieval and records version provenance without a second maintained value store.

optionExplanations.A: A date preference leaves superseded catalogues inside active retrieval and does not meet the one-authority requirement.
optionExplanations.B: Copying product values into the procedure violates the requirement not to maintain a second configuration copy.
optionExplanations.C: Duplicated dimensions in rules create a second changing value store and potential conflicting authority.
optionExplanations.D: R supplies current reference authority, separate history and draft-level version traceability.

questions.stemMarkdown:
An events team has two research tasks using public information. A booking assistant needs today’s published opening hours for one named conference venue before a call in five minutes. The venue has an official visitor page. If that page is unclear, the assistant can flag the uncertainty during the call rather than make a reservation.

A programme manager separately needs a briefing by tomorrow comparing how six venues have handled accessibility complaints over the past two years. She wants patterns, differences between provider statements and published visitor evidence, and gaps that prevent a firm conclusion. The relevant information is spread across venue pages, published reports, and dated accounts. Nobody has assembled it into a single reliable source.

The team has an approved lightweight live-search mode and a research mode that searches iteratively across many sources. Both can cite pages, and either output will be checked before use. There is time for the broader briefing, but the first task’s deadline is fixed.

Which allocation best fits the evidence needs and deadlines?

options.textMarkdown: Use lightweight live search for both tasks, asking for direct citations and uncertainty labels. The six-venue comparison can be assembled from each venue’s most relevant search result.
Use lightweight live search on the official page for the immediate lookup, and iterative research for the comparison, specifying source types, dates, and gaps to report.
Use iterative research for both tasks, narrowing the first to the official venue page. Applying one research method keeps evidence standards consistent across the team’s outputs.
Use lightweight live search for the immediate lookup and pretrained synthesis for the comparison. Search can then verify the specific claims identified in the completed comparative draft.

questions.explanationMarkdown: A five-minute current-hours lookup calls for lightweight search of the official page. The multi-venue historical comparison requires iterative research across dated provider and visitor evidence, with gaps made explicit.

optionExplanations.A: A single relevant result per venue is insufficient for the requested historical patterns and conflicting evidence.
optionExplanations.B: This matches the immediate factual lookup and the broader synthesis to their deadlines and evidence needs.
optionExplanations.C: Iterative research adds unnecessary latency to a simple lookup with a fixed five-minute deadline.
optionExplanations.D: Pretrained synthesis cannot establish the dispersed historical evidence and gaps the comparison requires.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A warehouse wants a 06:00 exception report even when staff laptops are shut down. The report must use stock transactions through 05:30 that morning and appear as a dated file in the shared reports folder. It only reports exceptions; it does not change inventory or contact suppliers.

IT has tested the following components. Each access route is approved for this data and purpose.

| Component | Tested availability and limits |
| --- | --- |
| Cloud scheduler and report worker | Runs at 06:00 without a staff device; can use approved cloud connections |
| Desktop transaction bridge | Reads the live warehouse system only while the analyst’s laptop is online |
| Managed cloud export | Completes at 05:40; includes transactions through 05:30; a completion marker identifies the export date and cutoff |
| Prior-day cloud snapshot | Always reachable; contains transactions only through 17:00 the previous day |
| Shared reports connection | Reachable from the cloud worker; can create files and return a destination file reference |

If the managed export is missing or has the wrong cutoff, the workflow must report that failure instead of presenting an older snapshot as the current report.

Which design meets the freshness, availability, and delivery requirements?

options.textMarkdown: Schedule the cloud worker to use the desktop bridge, with the prior-day snapshot as a fallback. Include the source timestamp in the dated report for staff review.
Schedule the cloud worker to use the managed export and save through the shared connection. Treat the scheduler’s completed status as confirmation that the report was delivered.
Schedule the cloud worker to check the managed export’s date and cutoff, create the report through the shared connection, and record delivery or an explicit failure.
Schedule the desktop bridge to prepare a cloud copy whenever the laptop is online. Let the 06:00 worker use the newest available copy and record its timestamp.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Only the managed export is both cloud-reachable and fresh enough. The worker must verify its date and cutoff, save through the reachable destination, and record actual delivery or explicit failure rather than equating scheduler status with success.

optionExplanations.A: The desktop bridge depends on the laptop, and the fallback is too old for the required cutoff.
optionExplanations.B: The source and destination are suitable, but scheduler completion does not establish freshness or actual delivery.
optionExplanations.C: Checking the export marker and recording delivery or failure meets freshness, availability and observable completion.
optionExplanations.D: The newest available desktop copy is not guaranteed to contain the specified morning cutoff.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A library asks AI to draft a quotation for a community group hiring recording equipment. Use only the approved hire terms below. Do not make a booking or promise availability. The supplied quote does not establish whether equipment is available on the requested date.

| Approved term | Source wording |
| --- | --- |
| Hire charge | Equipment hire is $240. A refundable $60 deposit is collected separately and is not part of the hire charge. |
| Cancellation | The hire charge is fully refundable when cancellation is received at least five calendar days before collection. |
| Changes | A request to change the collection date is subject to equipment availability. |

The AI draft states:

> The hire charge is $240, with a separate refundable deposit of $60. You can cancel for a full refund at least five calendar days before collection. If your plans change, you may move collection to any other date without a further charge.

The librarian wants the draft corrected to express only commitments established by the terms, while retaining the supported price information.

Which TWO independent corrections to the rescheduling statement are required?

options.textMarkdown: Explain that a change of collection date is a request subject to equipment availability, rather than a right to choose any other collection date.
State that date changes must be requested at least five calendar days before collection, applying the same notice period used for full cancellation refunds.
Remove the price figures until date availability has been checked, because an unconfirmed collection date prevents the approved hire charge from supporting a quotation.
Replace the unrestricted date-change statement with advice to cancel and make a new booking. The cancellation rule establishes the route for obtaining another collection date.
Remove the assurance that a collection-date change carries no further charge, because the supplied terms do not establish whether changing the date affects charges.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The change clause establishes a request conditional on availability, not a guaranteed new date. It says nothing about charges for changing dates. A and E remove those independent unsupported commitments while preserving supported price information.

optionExplanations.A: This restores the explicit availability condition on a date-change request.
optionExplanations.B: The five-day condition concerns cancellation refunds, not requests to change collection dates.
optionExplanations.C: The approved price supports a draft quotation without promising availability or making a booking.
optionExplanations.D: The cancellation clause does not establish cancel-and-rebook as the required date-change route.
optionExplanations.E: Removing the no-further-charge assurance avoids inventing a pricing term absent from the source.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A maintenance team expects a dated incident digest in its shared reports folder every Monday. The scheduled worker may read incident records and create a draft file. It cannot change incident data or send messages. These permissions and the source route were approved for this workflow.

Today’s expected digest is missing. The supervisor checks the run record before changing anything. The records connection is reachable and returned the requested incident rows. Usage allowance remains available. A previous folder test created a file successfully, and today’s log contains no write attempt.

The worker found two conflicting reporting-period labels in the supplied brief. It prepared a draft but stopped to ask which label to use. The run console displays “started”; the detailed state is “awaiting input.” The prompt asking for a period decision remains unanswered. The supervisor has authority to settle that label and resume the same run.

What should the supervisor do NEXT to complete and verify this run?

options.textMarkdown: Review the two period labels, answer the pending question, and resume the run. Then check the dated digest in the shared folder against the requested period.
Reauthorize the reports connection and repeat its write test before restarting the run. A successful test would establish that the missing digest can reach the intended folder.
Start a new run with a clarified reporting label, retaining the same incident rows. Leave the waiting run untouched until the new digest has been checked.
Revise the worker to choose a period label automatically and rerun the job. Check the new digest’s contents before allowing staff to use the weekly report.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The detailed run state identifies the immediate blockage: a pending period decision. The authorized supervisor should resolve it, resume the same run and inspect the actual dated file and reporting period.

optionExplanations.A: This resolves the recorded waiting state and then checks the requested deliverable.
optionExplanations.B: No write was attempted and the workflow is waiting for input; reauthorization does not remove that blockage.
optionExplanations.C: A new run is unnecessary when the supervisor can settle the question and resume the existing one.
optionExplanations.D: Automatic period selection changes the workflow's decision boundary instead of answering the current authorized question.

questions.stemMarkdown:
An adult-learning centre needs a shortlist of three evening first-aid courses for its volunteer coordinators. It can spend no more than $90 per participant, sessions must start after 18:00, and participants must be able to attend in person within the city. Registration must currently be open. The centre needs a table with course name, provider, total participant cost, dates, location, and evidence for each condition. Missing information should be marked, and no enrolments should be made.

The administrator knows two large providers and has drafted a recipe that tells AI which pages to open and which navigation links to follow. Those providers are possible choices, but there is no requirement to use them. Local charities may also offer suitable courses.

The administrator can check the resulting shortlist before recommending it. She wants AI to choose how to find candidates, while keeping the actual course limits and completion criteria clear.

Which brief best preserves those requirements while delegating the search method?

options.textMarkdown: Find qualifying courses at the two known providers and use the required evidence table. If fewer than three qualify, explain the remaining gaps before requesting a wider search.

Survey local training providers and recommend the three most promising courses, considering cost, timing, location, and registration. Include the required table so the administrator can make the final tradeoffs.
Find three currently open courses that meet the stated cost, timing, and location limits; supply the required evidence table, mark unresolved fields, and report if fewer qualify.
Follow the named providers’ booking pages to establish three qualifying courses, recording evidence in the required table. You may vary navigation steps and compare other local providers afterward.

questions.explanationMarkdown: An outcome brief retains every hard course condition and evidence requirement while letting AI choose the search method. C also handles fewer than three qualifying results without relaxing criteria or making enrollments.

optionExplanations.A: Limiting the initial search to two providers restricts the delegated method without a business requirement.
optionExplanations.B: Treating mandatory limits as considerations lets the AI return promising but nonqualifying courses.
optionExplanations.C: This preserves all limits, required evidence and honest shortfalls while delegating candidate discovery.
optionExplanations.D: Starting with named booking pages unnecessarily constrains the search and risks assuming three qualifying options exist there.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A youth arts charity collected parents’ email addresses to arrange workshop attendance and send schedule changes. Its collection notice covers those uses. A charity policy requires the data owner to approve any additional use of identifiable contact records before staff process them for that purpose.

The charity has an approved AI workspace, a read-only contact-record connection, and a separate staff-controlled messaging system. Both the workspace and the connection are approved for attendance administration. A coordinator now wants AI to combine contact records with attendance history to rank parents for fundraising invitations. The data owner has not considered that purpose.

No records have been retrieved for the fundraising task, and no invitations have been drafted or sent. The coordinator proposes to keep AI read-only and have the fundraising manager approve every invitation before sending. She asks whether those controls are enough to begin the ranking step using the existing records.

Which action best addresses the outstanding requirement before ranking begins?

options.textMarkdown: Use the approved connection to prepare the ranking, then ask the data owner to approve the invitations. Keeping the analysis internal allows the purpose review before messages leave.
Ask the data owner whether this fundraising use of contact and attendance records is covered or may be authorized; settle the applicable data-and-purpose approval before retrieval.
Obtain the fundraising manager’s approval of the ranking criteria and every invitation. That review links the new activity to an accountable person before any external contact occurs.
Replace parents’ names with stable IDs and produce the ranking in the attendance workspace. Keep the mapping with staff and ask the data owner before sending invitations.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The new ranking purpose has not been authorized for identifiable contact and attendance records. Data-owner approval must be settled before retrieval or processing; read-only access and later message approval do not authorize that new purpose.

optionExplanations.A: Ranking already processes records for the unapproved purpose before the data owner is asked.
optionExplanations.B: This settles the stated data-and-purpose authorization before the first processing step.
optionExplanations.C: The fundraising manager's review does not substitute for the required data owner's purpose approval.
optionExplanations.D: Stable IDs still allow linking to people, and postponing authorization until sending is too late for ranking.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A regional caterer wants AI to improve its stock-problem reporting. The operations director’s request is “give us something useful every week.” Existing records contain stock quantities, delivery delays, and purchase costs. They are current and approved for analysis, and the technical team can produce tables or dashboards from them.

The site managers want a Monday list of ingredients likely to run short before Friday. Procurement wants a Friday comparison of suppliers’ delivery performance. Finance wants a monthly account of waste costs. None of these requests was approved as the meaning of the director’s original instruction. The director can settle the priority and assign an owner.

A designer suggests building a combined dashboard so everyone gets a view. The project lead has one week to agree what the first release must achieve before construction begins. Existing sample records are available for checking whether the agreed output would answer its intended business question.

Which next action provides the soundest basis for the first release?

options.textMarkdown: Prototype the combined dashboard from the sample records and ask each team to mark useful views. Use their responses to settle release scope after the first build.
Present the competing uses and a sample output for each to the director. Settle the first release’s audience, business question, timing, inputs, and acceptance check.
Ask each team to rank the proposed views and build the highest-ranked combination. Keep the director as release approver and test the figures against sample records.
Use the director’s weekly timing to select the Monday stock-risk list. Record that interpretation, validate its figures, and request confirmation when the first report is ready.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Useful reporting has several competing meanings. Before construction, the director must settle the first release's audience, question, timing, inputs and acceptance check; example outputs help make that choice concrete.

optionExplanations.A: Building a combined dashboard first postpones the unsettled scope decision until after construction.
optionExplanations.B: The director can resolve the competing needs, and samples support a specific testable task definition.
optionExplanations.C: Team voting does not replace the director's authority to settle the release priority and owner.
optionExplanations.D: Weekly timing alone does not establish that Monday stock risk is the intended business question.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A facilities company is deciding between one central support desk and support staff assigned to each site. Neither structure has been approved. The decision criteria are total cost, response time, continuity during absences, and handover errors. Current figures are attached; forecasts are labelled estimates, and no weighting gives either structure an automatic advantage.

The proposed prompt is:

> Our plan to centralize support looks like the sensible next step. Compare it with keeping staff at each site using the four criteria. Find the strongest case for consolidation, identify manageable objections, and write a recommendation that helps leadership move the plan forward.

The analyst will replace the whole prompt rather than add a second instruction beneath it.

Which TWO replacement prompts independently permit an evidence-led decision while preserving the agreed comparison?

options.textMarkdown: Compare both structures on the four criteria. Credit consolidation’s forecast savings in full, and recognize site-based benefits when demonstrated in current records; state uncertainties in a separate note.

Compare both structures on the four criteria using the attached evidence. Distinguish estimates from established results, explain tradeoffs, and allow either recommendation or an unresolved conclusion.

Evaluate both structures against the four criteria and explain weaknesses in each. Require stronger evidence for a site-based recommendation because centralization is the proposal currently being considered.
Score both structures on the four criteria using the evidence, then recommend a hybrid to balance their strengths. Identify the additional facts needed to refine that compromise.
Apply the same evidence standard to each structure across the four criteria. Give the strongest case against each, mark unsupported claims, and explain which conclusion the evidence supports.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Both B and E replace biased framing with symmetrical evaluation on the four agreed criteria. Each lets evidence determine the outcome instead of fixing centralization, a stricter standard for one option, or a hybrid conclusion.

optionExplanations.A: Full credit for forecast savings but demonstrated-only credit for site benefits applies unequal evidence standards.
optionExplanations.B: This retains the comparison, separates estimates from results and permits either option or an unresolved finding.
optionExplanations.C: Requiring stronger evidence for site-based support biases the decision toward centralization.
optionExplanations.D: Mandating a hybrid fixes a third outcome before the comparison establishes it is appropriate.
optionExplanations.E: Equal evidence standards and challenges to each option allow an evidence-supported conclusion without a preferred structure.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A mailroom has a script that calculates parcel charges. The approved rule is $4 for the first 500 grams and $2 for each additional started block of 500 grams. Only dispatched parcels are charged. A missing weight must be excluded from the total and listed as an exception. Weights may be in grams or kilograms.

The script has passed an independently checked test containing three dispatched parcels, each weighing 400 grams. The manager wants a further check before relying on its monthly charge report.

| Small test file | Status | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Dispatched | 0.75 kg |
| M2 | Dispatched | 1,200 g |
| M3 | Returned | 1.80 kg |
| M4 | Dispatched | Missing |

The manager has worked through this file independently: M1 costs $6, M2 costs $8, M3 is uncharged, and M4 belongs in the exception list. The expected charge total is $14.

Which check would provide the strongest additional validation of the required behaviours?

options.textMarkdown: Match charges by parcel ID against $6 and $8, reconcile $14, and verify that M3 is uncharged and M4 alone appears in the missing-weight exception list.
Compare totals for kilogram and gram entries against $6 and $8, reconcile $14, and confirm the report contains two charged parcels and one missing-weight exception.
Run the file in both original and reversed order. Confirm $14, two charged parcels, and M4 as the sole exception in each independently checked report.
Match M1 and M2’s reported charges against $6 and $8, reconcile $14, and confirm that two parcels are uncharged and one exception has been recorded.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The strongest check tests each required behavior against an independently worked answer: M1=$6, M2=$8, M3 uncharged, M4 alone excepted and total=$14. A explicitly verifies parcel identities as well as totals and exception handling.

optionExplanations.A: This checks the two specific charges, the total, the returned parcel exclusion and the exact exception identity.
optionExplanations.B: Unit-group totals and counts do not explicitly establish that M3 is uncharged or that M4 is the particular exception.
optionExplanations.C: Order invariance and a correct total do not establish each parcel's required charge; compensating errors can survive.
optionExplanations.D: Charges and aggregate counts do not establish that M3, rather than another parcel, is the returned uncharged case or that M4 is the exception.

questions.stemMarkdown:
An engineering partnership needs an index of scanned drawings in an approved workstation folder. The index must contain drawing identifiers, published titles, revision marks, and a list of unclear marks. The workstation will remain on; no unattended cloud workflow is needed.

The signed data agreement keeps scans, drawing identifiers, and revision information on that workstation. It permits published title text to be processed by one approved hosted service. That service can normalize titles and format index rows.

IT has tested an offline worker that reads the scans, matches fields by drawing, reviews unclear marks locally, and builds a searchable index. It can exchange selected fields with the hosted service. A local review tool can also obtain a hosted second opinion on cropped images, and a desktop tool offers automatic hosted troubleshooting reports containing extracted rows.

Each proposed workflow can produce the index. The engineer must select a processing path within the existing agreement.

Which option fits the task and the established processing boundary?

options.textMarkdown: Extract fields locally and remove drawing identifiers before sending title-and-revision rows to the approved formatter. Restore identifiers and save the completed index on the workstation.
Send published titles to the approved service for normalization. Keep field matching, revision checks, unclear-mark review, and assembly of the searchable index within the offline worker.
Use the desktop tool to extract and assemble the index locally, with automatic troubleshooting reports enabled. Keep source scans in the restricted folder and review unclear marks.
Use the offline worker for extraction and indexing, with the local review tool obtaining second opinions on unclear crops. Retain every full scan and completed index locally.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The agreement permits only published title text to reach the hosted service. B uses that permission while keeping scans, identifiers, revision checks, unclear crops and index assembly local; local files or tools do not guarantee local processing.

optionExplanations.A: Revision information would be transmitted along with titles, violating the stated hosted-processing limit.
optionExplanations.B: Only permitted title text goes to the hosted service; all restricted information and processing remain local.
optionExplanations.C: Automatic hosted troubleshooting reports contain extracted rows, sending restricted information outside the workstation.
optionExplanations.D: A cropped scan is still scan content, and hosted second opinions breach the processing boundary.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A community transport service has 40 additional weekly places. Its approved priority rule considers mobility need and lack of another transport option. AI proposes a shortlist; the service manager can inspect all applications and change it before places are offered. Data access is approved, and no offers have been sent.

A trial used applications from two referral routes. Staff checked the accuracy of the information extracted from every application. The ranking prompt also asked AI to assess “strength of the applicant’s case.” Applications from route Y were submitted through translated forms and tended to have shorter explanations.

| Referral route | Applications | Selected for proposed places |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| X | 80 | 32 |
| Y | 80 | 8 |

The two routes have similar distributions of recorded mobility need and alternative transport. No review has yet compared ranking reasons or the treatment of short explanations. The manager wants to investigate the disparity without assuming equal selection rates are required.

Which TWO compatible controls most directly investigate whether the ranking gives applicants fair treatment under the approved rule?

options.textMarkdown: Replace the proposed split with 20 places per route and review the selected applications against the recorded needs. This prevents referral route from determining the allocation.
Obtain a second model’s shortlist using the same prompt and compare the route split. Agreement would distinguish a stable priority pattern from variation between individual runs.

Inspect ranking reasons to see whether writing detail or translated wording affected priority beyond the approved needs. Where that occurs, correct the criterion and re-evaluate affected applications.
Review selected and excluded applications from both routes, including short explanations and cases near the cutoff. Compare their treatment against the same mobility and transport conditions.
Ask the manager to read every selected application before offers are sent, checking its recorded needs. Retain unsuccessful applications so a later complaint can trigger another review.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The disparity is a signal to investigate, rather than proof that equal quotas are required. C checks whether writing or translation introduced an unauthorized ranking criterion; D compares both selections and exclusions against the same approved needs.

optionExplanations.A: Equal allocation by route introduces a quota the approved priority rule does not require and does not diagnose ranking reasons.
optionExplanations.B: Two models can reproduce the same prompt-induced disadvantage; agreement does not establish fair application of the rule.
optionExplanations.C: Examining ranking reasons tests whether irrelevant writing features displaced the approved priorities.
optionExplanations.D: Reviewing both selected and excluded cases, including boundary cases, tests consistent application across routes.
optionExplanations.E: Reviewing only selected applications cannot reveal wrongly excluded applicants or the cause of the disparity.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A service centre introduced an AI-assisted job-routing process at the same time as two experienced supervisors began working extra shifts. The centre wants AI to summarize what changed. The source counts cover two four-week periods with the same number of completed jobs, the same delay definition, and a similar job mix. Neither change was tested separately.

| Recorded measure | Before both changes | After both changes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Completed jobs | 200 | 200 |
| Jobs exceeding the agreed turnaround | 40 | 24 |

The AI summary says:

> Delayed jobs fell by 40%, from 40 to 24. This demonstrates that AI routing produced the whole improvement. The centre can expect the same reduction when the extra supervisor shifts end.

The figures and introduction dates have been independently checked. No further evidence distinguishes the contribution of routing from that of the extra shifts.

Which evaluation of the summary is best supported?

options.textMarkdown: Retain the 40% reduction as the AI-routing result, but qualify the forecast because the same improvement may not recur. The matched job mix supports attribution to routing.
Retain the measured reduction, describe it as following the combined changes, and withhold attribution to routing alone or the forecast until evidence separates their contributions.
Describe the two changes as jointly responsible for a 40% reduction, splitting the improvement equally in the report. Mark each share provisional until another period is reviewed.
Treat the extra shifts as the leading explanation and remove routing from the improvement finding. Experienced supervision provides a more direct mechanism for resolving delayed jobs.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The reduction is 16/40 = 40%, and the matched periods support that descriptive result. Because routing and extra shifts changed together, the evidence does not isolate either cause or establish that the reduction will persist without the shifts.

optionExplanations.A: Similar job mix does not separate routing's contribution from the simultaneously added supervision.
optionExplanations.B: This preserves the verified descriptive change and withholds unsupported exclusive attribution and forecast.
optionExplanations.C: An equal causal split is invented; no evidence estimates the contribution of either change.
optionExplanations.D: Plausibility of supervision as a mechanism does not establish it as the leading cause or exclude routing.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A printing cooperative uses an AI-written script to combine weekly order exports. It handles repeated order IDs, keeps the final status, and lists unreadable rows. The operations analyst checked its results against a small week she had already reconciled. The current script produced the correct totals and exception list.

Another analyst will take over next month. He is authorized to use the same folder and runtime, which IT has confirmed will remain available. He needs to repeat the task without the original chat. Six months later, the cooperative may change the status rule, and someone must be able to understand why the existing result was produced and check an edited version.

The current chat contains several discarded scripts and the final one. The latest report is available, but its totals alone do not show which input rules created them. The analyst wants a small, dependable handoff package.

Which package best supports repeat use and later controlled changes?

options.textMarkdown: Save the final script and the latest report with a quick-start note. The report provides a reference result, while the script preserves the order-processing logic.
Save a complete export of the chat, label its successful run, and add the next week’s input format. Future analysts can locate the code and reconstruct its rules.
Save the verified script, a plain-language brief of its inputs and rules, and the checked sample with expected outputs together. Include a clear run instruction.
Save the approved brief and checked sample with expected outputs, then generate a new script from them each week. Compare the sample result before processing new exports.

questions.explanationMarkdown: A dependable handoff retains the verified implementation, the intent and input rules, and a known-answer sample with run instructions. That supports immediate reuse and later changes without reconstructing discarded chat versions.

optionExplanations.A: The latest report alone is not a documented input-rule brief or reusable checked input-and-expected-output test.
optionExplanations.B: A chat export forces successors to reconstruct the intended version and rules from discarded alternatives.
optionExplanations.C: The verified script, explicit brief, checked sample and run instruction support repeatability and controlled maintenance.
optionExplanations.D: Regenerating weekly discards the stable verified implementation and introduces avoidable rule or code drift.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A sports retailer asks AI for weekly category totals from a clean sales export. The brief states the source columns, currency, refund signs, inclusion rule, and required output. A finance analyst confirms that those instructions are complete and that the source is current.

Across three fresh conversations using the same model and brief, AI identifies the correct eligible records but produces slightly different sums. Manually checked category totals are available. Repeating the rules and asking for intermediate arithmetic has not removed the discrepancy. The other parts of each report meet the requested format.

The current mode writes calculations as text. An approved execution mode can run code on the same export and return the computed figures. The model, inputs, and business rules can be held constant. The manager wants a small diagnostic comparison before changing the shared brief or choosing a different model.

Which test most clearly distinguishes the suspected cause?

options.textMarkdown: Repeat the report in a new conversation with only the finance rules and sales export. Compare its totals with the manually checked figures to reduce accumulated-context effects.
Ask a stronger model to produce the same totals using execution mode, then compare them with the checked figures. A passing result would support that upgraded configuration.
Require a row-by-row written calculation in the current mode and compare each subtotal with the checked figures. Correct the first mismatch before requesting the full report.
Use the execution mode with the same model, export, and rules, then compare computed totals with the checked figures. Leave the shared brief unchanged for this test.

questions.explanationMarkdown: The prompt and fresh-session checks already passed, while repeated arithmetic errors arise in text calculation. Holding the model, inputs and rules constant and changing only execution mode most directly tests the feature hypothesis against known totals.

optionExplanations.A: Fresh sessions have already shown the error, so this repeats a check that does not isolate the suspected feature.
optionExplanations.B: Changing both model and execution mode cannot distinguish which change addresses the error.
optionExplanations.C: A written replay remains text arithmetic and does not test whether actual execution fixes the repeatable error.
optionExplanations.D: This changes the suspected feature alone and compares its output with independently checked results.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A commercial property team is designing a rent-credit workflow for disputed service charges. The finance lead is answerable for each credit that becomes part of an issued invoice. The source facts can all be supplied through an approved environment. Computing a proposed credit and authorizing that credit are separate steps; no credits have been issued during this design review.

The table records design decisions in the order made.

| Decision | Design record |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Confirmed that this data and purpose are approved for the environment and that every input needed for the calculation is available. |
| 2 | Assigned both proposed-credit calculation and final credit authorization to AI, because a script can reproduce the formula exactly. |
| 3 | Selected code execution and a saved procedure for the calculations, with known-answer tests before use. |
| 4 | Assigned the finance lead to review the issued invoices at day end and investigate any disputed credit then. |

The team is reviewing the design before implementation.

Which decision FIRST misapplies the course’s method for assigning work?

options.textMarkdown: Decision 2: reliable computation is an implementation property; it does not settle who owns the consequential authorization. Classify those two steps separately before selecting what carries them.
Decision 1: approved data and available inputs establish technical access rather than task suitability. Require a completed production trial before allowing the ownership decisions to proceed.
Decision 4: review after invoice issue leaves the consequential credit unchecked beforehand. Move the finance lead’s decision to a point before the credit affects an issued invoice.
Decision 3: known-answer tests show that the selected formula works on examples. Select the model for the entire credit workflow before choosing code and a procedure.

questions.explanationMarkdown: Decision 2 first conflates computation reliability with ownership of consequential authorization. Calculation and final authorization must be classified separately; decision 4 is also poorly timed but occurs later.

optionExplanations.A: Exact computation does not make AI the accountable decision-maker for final invoice credits.
optionExplanations.B: The data and input eligibility checks are appropriate prerequisites, rather than an ownership failure requiring a production trial first.
optionExplanations.C: Post-issue review is a real later weakness, but decision 2 is the first erroneous assignment.
optionExplanations.D: Code and known-answer tests fit the calculation step; model choice does not settle authorization ownership.
